analysis.one_liner: Caps interest on consumer loans at 36% by extending military lending protections to everyone.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 26 cosponsors but never got a committee vote or floor vote; it sat in the House Financial Services Committee until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Members of the military already have a federal law, the Military Lending Act, that caps the interest rate on their loans at 36% a year and bans common fee tricks. This bill would extend those same protections to every American consumer, with a few exceptions: home mortgages, car and personal-property purchase loans, and loans from federal credit unions. It also lets state attorneys general enforce the rule and blocks regulators from carving out exemptions for lenders.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary borrowers, especially people with poor or thin credit who are offered payday loans, auto title loans, and subprime credit cards at rates far above 36%. Service members already have this cap; this bill would give the same shield to veterans and civilians. People who are currently charged triple-digit annual interest rates would pay far less to borrow, and lenders could no longer bury the true cost in credit-insurance fees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Veterans, service members, and low-income borrowers

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual percentage rate on most consumer credit at 36% by applying Military Lending Act rules to all consumers [S2][S3].
Counts credit insurance premiums and similar add-on fees toward the interest rate, so lenders cannot hide the real cost of a loan [S3].
Lets state attorneys general and state regulators sue lenders that break the rule, and preserves state laws that protect consumers more strongly [S3].
Blocks the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau from granting exemptions to the rate cap [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Payday and auto title lenders, whose business model depends on rates of 300% or more a year, would lose their core product. Subprime credit card issuers and sellers of credit insurance would also lose revenue. Some high-risk borrowers could find fewer lenders willing to serve them at all.

drawbacks.text: A 36% cap can make lending to the riskiest borrowers unprofitable, so some people with bad credit could be denied loans entirely and pushed toward informal or illegal borrowing — a tradeoff an honest supporter has to acknowledge [S2].
The bill leaves gaps: home mortgages and secured car and personal-property purchase loans are exempt, and a secured car loan can still carry hidden dealer markups [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Extending a rate cap that Congress already judged appropriate for soldiers and their families to all borrowers is a strong protection against debt traps, and the bill adds state enforcement and closes the fee-hiding loopholes. The real cost is that some of the riskiest borrowers may lose access to formal credit altogether. That tradeoff is real, but the military version of this rule has been in force without collapsing credit for service members.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced in November 2019, and the committee never took it up or sent it to the floor before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Chuy Garcia introduced the Veterans and Consumers Fair Credit Act in the House on November 12, 2019 [S1][S5].
The bill would cap consumer credit interest rates at 36% by applying Military Lending Act protections to all consumers [S2].
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction [S5].

It gathered 26 cosponsors — 25 Democrats and 1 Republican — but the action history shows no further steps: no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday, title, and other high-rate lenders, who kept charging triple-digit annual interest rates to ordinary borrowers, and the committee members who never had to vote on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-rate lenders kept charging; no one had to vote

for.name: Rep. Jesus "Chuy" Garcia
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on November 12, 2019.

for.name: Rep. Glenn Grothman
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

for.name: 1 of 197 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: The only House Republican to cosponsor the bill.

against.name: Maxine Waters
against.what_they_did: Her committee received the bill on referral in November 2019 and never scheduled a markup or reported it out before the Congress ended.

against.name: Payday and installment lending industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed national 36% rate caps, which would eliminate their core loan products.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided: 25 Democrats and 1 Republican signed on, and no vote was ever held to test broader party support.

industries.note: These lenders charge annual rates commonly in the hundreds of percent; a 36% cap ends their core product. Their revenue depends on charging ordinary borrowers far more than other credit costs [S2].
Cards marketed to weak-credit borrowers often exceed 36% APR once fees are counted; the bill caps those rates and counts credit-insurance fees toward the finance charge [S3].

industries.industry: Credit insurance and add-on product sellers
industries.note: Single-premium credit insurance and debt-cancellation fees would be counted in the interest rate, making many of these add-ons unworkable [S3].
Federal credit union loans are exempt from the cap and remain subject to the credit union usury limit, giving them a relative advantage over nonmember lenders [S3].
